meta.titre: Chemical Composition of Food: Elements, Building Blocks and Why Each Nutrient Matters
meta.sous_theme: Carbohydrates, fats and proteins: elements, building blocks, tests and uses

sections.contenu_markdown:
In the market, a woman sells cassava, groundnuts and beans side by side. All three feed the family, but they do not do the same job in the body.
Cassava gives mostly energy, groundnuts give oil as well as protein, and beans are rich in protein.
GCE Biology asks which elements a nutrient contains, what its building blocks are, what it does in the body and which reagent shows it in a food.
This course puts these facts in one place and shows how to build a full answer.

items: Food provides energy and the materials for growth and repair.
Elements are the simple substances from which all matter is made, for example carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen.
A test tube can be heated safely in a water bath.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Elements, building blocks and roles

| Nutrient | Elements | Building blocks | Main uses in the body | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Carbohydrates | Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen | Simple sugars such as glucose | Source of energy | Cassava, yam, rice, maize, plantain |
| Fats and oils | Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen (proportionally less oxygen than a carbohydrate) | Fatty acids and glycerol | Energy store, insulation under the skin, protection of organs | Palm oil, groundnuts, meat fat |
| Proteins | Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen (sometimes sulphur) | Amino acids | Growth and repair, enzymes, antibodies, some hormones | Beans, fish, eggs, meat |

In a carbohydrate the hydrogen and oxygen atoms are in the same ratio as in water, two hydrogen atoms to one oxygen atom. Only proteins contain **nitrogen**, so nitrogen separates proteins from the other two.

### Why proteins matter
Children need protein to grow and to build new cells. Adults need it to repair worn or damaged tissue. Enzymes and antibodies are proteins. A child who gets too little protein over a long time may suffer from a deficiency disease called kwashiorkor.

### Food tests

| Nutrient | Reagent and method | Positive result |
|---|---|---|
| Starch | Add iodine solution | Brown or yellow changes to blue-black |
| Reducing sugar | Add Benedict's solution and heat in a water bath | Blue changes to green, yellow, orange, then brick red |
| Protein | Add Millon's reagent and warm gently (the reagent is poisonous) | Red colour |
| Protein | Add dilute sodium hydroxide, then a few drops of copper(II) sulphate (biuret test) | Purple or violet |
| Fat | Shake the food with ethanol, then pour the clear liquid into water | Cloudy white emulsion |

Crush a solid food with water before testing.

variantes.nom: Reading a set of test results
variantes.quand_utiliser: When colours are given and the nutrients must be named
variantes.contenu_markdown: Take the tests one at a time. A positive colour proves the nutrient is present. If the original colour of the reagent remains, say that the nutrient was not detected. Never mix up the reagents: iodine is for starch only.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When masses of nutrients in a sample are given
variantes.contenu_markdown: $$\text{percentage} = \frac{\text{mass of nutrient}}{\text{total mass}} \times 100$$ The remainder of the sample is water, minerals and other substances.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks for uses of a nutrient to the body
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give separate uses, each with a short reason: 'Proteins build new cells, so children grow.' Do not repeat the same use in different words.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A food sample X was crushed in water and divided into four portions. The results were:

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Iodine solution | Blue-black |
| Benedict's solution, heated | Stayed blue |
| Millon's reagent, warmed | Red |
| Ethanol, then water | Stayed clear |

(a) Name the nutrients present in X.

(b) Name the nutrients not detected in X.

(c) Name the element found in one of the nutrients in X but not in the other.

etapes.action: Link each reagent to its nutrient.
etapes.justification: Iodine detects starch, Benedict's detects reducing sugar, Millon's detects protein and ethanol with water detects fat.
A positive result is a colour change typical of that reagent.

etapes.action: State what each positive test shows.
etapes.justification: Blue-black shows starch. Red with Millon's shows protein.
Benedict's stayed blue and the ethanol mixture stayed clear.
etapes.resultat_markdown: No reducing sugar and no fat were detected.

etapes.action: Compare the elements of starch and protein.
etapes.justification: Starch is a carbohydrate containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Protein also contains nitrogen.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Nitrogen is in protein but not in starch.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) **Starch and protein.** (b) **Reducing sugar and fat.** (c) **Nitrogen**, found in protein only.

items.pourquoi_faux: Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only.
items.correction_markdown: Nitrogen is in proteins, not in carbohydrates or fats.

items.erreur_markdown: Iodine solution turns blue-black when sugar is present.
items.correction_markdown: Starch gives blue-black with iodine; reducing sugar gives a brick red colour with Benedict's after heating.

items.erreur_markdown: Benedict's solution stayed blue, so the food contains no carbohydrate.
items.pourquoi_faux: Benedict's detects only reducing sugars, and the sample may not have been heated. Starch and sucrose would not react even when heated.
items.correction_markdown: Say 'no reducing sugar detected' and test for starch with iodine as well.

items.erreur_markdown: Proteins are made of fatty acids and glycerol.
items.pourquoi_faux: Fatty acids and glycerol are the building blocks of fats.
items.correction_markdown: Proteins are made of amino acids.

items.erreur_markdown: Proteins are the body's chief source of energy.
items.pourquoi_faux: Carbohydrates are the chief energy source; the body uses protein mainly for growth and repair.
items.correction_markdown: Give growth and repair, enzymes and antibodies as the uses of protein.

items.enonce_markdown: Match each test to the nutrient it detects: (i) iodine solution, (ii) Benedict's solution, (iii) ethanol then water.
items.solution_markdown:
(i) Iodine solution detects **starch**.

(ii) Benedict's solution detects **reducing sugar**.

(iii) Ethanol then water detects **fat**.

items.enonce_markdown:
A dried food contains 62 g of carbohydrate, 18 g of protein and 12 g of fat in every 100 g. The rest is water and minerals.

(a) Calculate the mass of water and minerals in 100 g.

(b) Calculate the mass of protein in a 250 g bag of this food.

(c) Name the building blocks of the protein.
Describe how you would show that a groundnut seed contains both protein and fat. State the results you expect and one precaution.
items.solution_markdown:
**Protein:** crush the seed with a little water. Add dilute sodium hydroxide, then a few drops of dilute copper(II) sulphate solution. A **purple** colour shows protein. (Millon's reagent, warmed, gives a red colour.)

**Fat:** crush the seed, shake it with ethanol and filter. Pour the clear liquid into a test tube of water. A **cloudy white emulsion** shows fat.

Precaution: use clean apparatus and compare with a control in which water replaces the food. Keep reagents such as sodium hydroxide away from the skin and eyes.

items_markdown: Carbohydrates and fats contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen; proteins also contain nitrogen.
Building blocks: simple sugars for carbohydrates, fatty acids and glycerol for fats, amino acids for proteins.
Carbohydrates give energy; fats store energy and insulate; proteins give growth, repair, enzymes and antibodies.
Tests: iodine for starch, Benedict's with heat for reducing sugar, Millon's or biuret for protein, ethanol then water for fat.
A negative result means 'not detected'; report it as such.
Percentage = mass of nutrient / total mass x 100.
